Let $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(z-z_i)\in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $\lvert z_i\rvert < 1$ for all $i$. 
Must there always exist a path of length less than $2$ in\[\{z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}\]which connects two of the roots of $f$?
#1041: [EHP58,p.139]
analysis | 
polynomials
A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that this set always has a connected component containing at least two of the roots.

 I got Astra to write up a positive family for the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian path question in which the connecting path is explicit. This is separate from ani’s 7 September degree-seven counterexample claim in this thread; it is not a general path theorem.
Let
$$
f(z)=z^n+az^m+b,\qquad 1\le m\lt n,
$$
be monic, with every zero in the open unit disc. Every root can be joined to the origin by a straight segment contained in $\{|f|\lt 1\}$. Thus any two distinct roots $\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}$ are joined through the origin with length $|\zeta_{1}|+|\zeta_{2}|\lt 2$. Repeated root occurrences admit the constant path.
At a root $\zeta$, the root equation removes the middle coefficient before absolute values are taken:
$$
f(t\zeta)=b(1-t^m)+\zeta^n(t^n-t^m).
$$
Vieta gives $|b|\lt 1$, so for $0\le t\lt 1$,
$$
|f(t\zeta)|
\le |b|(1-t^m)+|\zeta|^n(t^m-t^n)
\lt 1-t^n\le1.
$$
At $t=1$, the value is zero. No flow-tree decomposition is needed. Pendyala’s degree-four theorem treats the general degree-four case under the original root-location hypothesis; this is instead a coefficient-restricted family with no degree bound.
Separately, the short paper proves the critical-value estimate
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|f(c_{j})|^{2/(n-1)}\le n-1
$$
for any monic degree-$n$ polynomial, $n\ge2$, with zeros in the closed unit disc, where the critical points $c_{j}$ are counted with multiplicity. It is sharp for $f(z)=z^n-\lambda$, $|\lambda|=1$. The reflected derivative bounds $|f(c_{j})|$ by $\prod_{k}|1-\overline{c_{k}}c_{j}|$; a weighted Poisson identity controls the resulting product mean. This bounds critical values, not the lengths of connecting paths.
Section 1 extends the same radial argument. For a degree-$n$ polynomial $f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{k}z^k$ and a root $\zeta$, set $S_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^j a_{k}\zeta^k$, $0\le j\lt n$. Abel summation puts $f(t\zeta)/(1-t^n)$, $0\le t\lt 1$, in the convex hull of these $S_{j}$. If they all lie in the open unit disc, the whole segment is certified. An explicit sextic shows that root location alone does not guarantee this prescribed radial path.
Separately, §3 proves that a squarefree monic polynomial of degree at least two with least critical-value modulus at most $13/25$ has some pair of distinct roots joined by a curve of length $\lt 2$ in $\{|f|\lt 1\}$, without a root-location assumption. The longer record gives the geometric proof and exact rational certificate, alongside obstructions to particular path constructions.
An earlier reference for the critical-value estimate, or a natural enlargement of the radial family, would be welcome.
The Abel identity, trinomial radial inequalities and bound $|\zeta_{1}|+|\zeta_{2}|\lt 2$ have public Lean source at the separate revision cited by the longer record. Assembling them into a rectifiable path remains an ordinary step. The critical-value and low-critical-value arguments are ordinary proofs, not end-to-end Lean theorems. The verification record identifies the separate Newton-flow, ray-separation, root-retention and selected family checks.
AI tools contributed substantially to the research, code and drafting under my direction. I am responsible for the claims and for correcting errors. These notes have not had independent mathematical review; formal checks apply only to the statements identified, not to novelty or to the papers as a whole.
This is one of eight Erdős problems in Plectis, not eight claimed solutions. The website links the other seven and shows the wider research environment I’m opening in stages. Further formalisation and supporting material are in progress. Results and unsuccessful approaches are kept together for reuse; corrections and ideas I use will be credited, with contributors’ agreement.

 I have proven the quartic case of this problem: if $f$ is monic of degree four and all zeros of $f$, counted with multiplicity, lie in the open unit disk, then two of these zeros can be joined inside
$$
{z : |f(z)| < 1}
$$
by a possibly degenerate polygonal path of length less than $2$.
The preprint is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24875. In addition, using the Aristotle AI based API, the result has been formalized and verified in Lean. I'm currently unsure of how exactly to share the Lean files for reproducibility and scrutiny, but if anyone is interested/or knows how to share them, I'm more than willing to post those.

 I'm willing to rate the argument as being plausibly correct. With regards to having publication-level quality of exposition and literature review, the manuscript still needs a lot of work however, on a number of fronts. Much of this is tied to the tendency of current-level AI writing to dwell far too much on routine results (often without citing relevant literature), or technical details, and not enough time emphasizing the high level structure.
In this case, the high-level structure is that there are four key results that resolve the Erdos problem, each of which is independently interesting:
1. The EHP component lemma (at least one component $U$ with two or more zeroes).
2. An integral bound $\int_U |f'(z)/f(z)|\ dA \leq 2\pi m$, where $m$ is the number of zeroes (Proposition 4).
3. A lemma asserting that on any given region $U$, there is a tree connecting the $m$ zeroes of $U$ (formed by following the Morse gradient flow on $\log |f|$, basically) of total length at most $\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_U |f'(z)/f(z)|\ dA$, at least assuming some technical non-degeneracy hypotheses on $f$. (Proposition 12)
4. A simple combinatorial lemma that asserts that any tree contains a path of length at most twice the total length of the tree, divided by the number of vertices of the tree. (Lemma 17)
There is also a technical
0. One can perturb $f$ to obey the non-degeneracy conditions required for the third ingredient to work. (Lemma 14)
Combining all these ingredients, the Erdos problem follows. But the AI-generated exposition spends a lot of time on the least interesting parts of this process (e.g., Step 0), and many steps could be proven much more quickly. For instance Lemma 3 is obvious because the level sets of $p$ are algebraic sets of dimension less than 2, and thus immediately of measure zero (e.g., by the Crofton formula). Several pages of argument are used to establish the formula $\int_{\varepsilon < u < t} |\nabla u|^2\ dA = 2\pi m(t-\varepsilon)$ on page 5, but this is just the area formula noting that $f$ is $m$-to-one on $U$, so (a suitable branch of) $\log f$ is also $m$-to-one mapping to a fundamental domain of $\{ \varepsilon < \mathrm{Re} z < t \}$.
I also suspect that there is a less convoluted way to arrive at Proposition 4 from this area formula and the Polya inequality than the one provided in the AI-generated text, although I have not tried too hard to locate such a simplified argument. Similarly, the perturbative component of the argument (Step 0) seems to occupy far more space in the AI-generated document than it needs to: I think the cleanest thing to do is first resolve the Erdos problem for "generic" polynomials f (perhaps with some sort of "padding") and use some sort of Rouche theorem argument to deduce the general case from this, instead of spend so much time constructing explicit perturbations of polynomials.
Finally, it's a bit concerning that the AI-generated article cites almost none of the extensive literature on lemniscates, and I suspect that many of the arguments here have precursors or other links to the literature that need to be explored; it may be that the AI tool implicitly relied upon such literature arguments without explicitly disclosing the connection. All of this would have to be resolved (preferably by a primarily human-generated document) before this result would be suitable for submission to a peer-reviewed journal.

 After working with Claude and doing some literature search, I have a shorter proof of Proposition 4 (Step 2). From the area formula (noting that $f$ is an $m$-fold map from $U$ to the disk) one has
$$ \int_U |f'(z)|^2 / |f(z)|^{2-1/m}\ dA(z) = m \int_{D(0,1)} 1/|w|^{2-1/m}\ dA(w) = 2 \pi m^2$$
so by Cauchy--Schwarz it suffices to show that
$$ \int_U |f(z)|^{-1/m}\ dA(z) \leq 2\pi.$$
By the layer-cake decomposition it suffices to show that the level sets $\{ z \in U: |f(z)| \leq s \}$ have area at most $\pi s^{2/m}$ for all $0 < s \leq 1$. By Theorem 1 of this paper of Dubinin (a Polya type inequality), this area is at most $s^{2/m}$ times the area of $U$; and by the classical Polya inequality, $U$ has area at most $\pi$. The claim follows.
The arguments used here and in the AI-generated article are also rather similar to those in this paper of Crane.
I'm going to look at Proposition 12 (Step 3) next. I have a suspicion that one does not need quite so much working out of the topology of the situation, and should be able to proceed by more purely analytic arguments; but I have not digested it yet.

 I can elaborate a bit further on why I am now pessimistic on the entire approach. The strategy is to try to connect zeroes of $f$ together by performing gradient flow on $u = \log \frac{1}{|f|}$, which is (locally at least) the same thing as working on level curves of the harmonic conjugate $\mathrm{arg} f$, and hoping that this creates a tree of short total length that one can then cut up (along an Eulerian path) to find a path connecting two zeroes together.
The problem is that this flow simply does not create trees, which becomes obvious once one generates a visual plot. Here is a plot of what the gradient flow lines look like for $f(z) = z^2-1$; the construction given is to basically take two arcs of the same color, which connect the two zeroes $\pm 1$ to the boundary of the region $U$ under consideration, but do not connect to each other. There is a critical point at $0$ that can connect the zeroes together, but only two flow lines go into that point and two flow lines go out, and a random flow line construction will never find this. (The integral $\int_U |f'/f|\ dA$, by the way, can be viewed as the average value of the total flow line length for a randomly chosen color.)

 This is quite interesting.
By Riemann-Hurwitz, a component of $\Lambda_f := \{z: |f(z)| < 1\}$ with $m$ zeros of $f$ will have $m-1$ zeros of $f'$. (Note: zeros must be counted with multiplicity.)

- There is a path in $U$ joining two roots of $f$ with length $< 2$.
- There is a path in $U$ joining a root of $f$ and a root of $f'$ with length $< 1$.

 Sendov's Conjecture is interesting. Having in mind the "musical chair" 
picture for roots and critical points of polynomial $f$ one can look at 
the following variant of Sendov's:
Let be $n \ge 1$. Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree n with zeros $z_1, ..., z_n$,
all in the complex unit ball. Let $f'$ be the derivative (thus with degree $n-1$) 
with roots $y_1$, ..., $y_{n-1}$. Add the auxiliary point $y_n = 0$.
** Conjecture: Then there exists a permutation $p$ of {1, 2, ..., n} 
such that distance $(x_i, y_{p(i)}) \le 1$ for $i=1, ..., n$. The 
condition for $i=n$ holds trivially, because $0$ is central in the 
unit ball. The interesting remaining cases are $i=1, ..., n-1$. **
The conjecture is in some sense weaker than Sendov's,
because $y_n$ gives a free meal for one root of $f$. But it is 
stronger than Sendov's in another sense, because all the 
other roots of $f$ need different near-distance $f'$-roots as 
their partners.
For $n=3$ the conjecture has a simple proof by Hall's 
marriage theorem.

A proof 
claimed by Borisov Alexey.
 Summary:
 Problem #1041
Claim: the cubic case admits a positive answer. If f(z) = (z−z₀)(z−z₁)(z−z₂) with |z_j| < 1, then two roots of f, counted with multiplicity, may be joined inside {|f| < 1} by a polygonal path of length < 2.
The argument relies on a local fact. Take a critical point c of a monic cubic and a root a with |f(c)| < 1 and |a − c| < 1. Then the whole segment from c to a remains in {|f| < 1}, since near a critical point the polynomial behaves locally like a cube and its modulus grows too slowly to reach 1 before the endpoint. So it suffices to find one critical point lying within distance 1 of two roots.
Such a point is obtained by centering the roots at their centroid and writing them as a_j = pω^j + qω^{−j} with ω = e^{2πi/3}. This yields |p|² + |q|² < 1, and the polynomial turns into a depressed cubic with explicit critical points. A brief trigonometric check produces the required path.
